title: Namo rudrāya viṣṇave: protection from death
theme: A one-line formula of homage to Rudra and Viṣṇu with a request for protection from death.

words.context: the anonymous commentator supplies the verb: «नमोऽस्तु»

words.role: by the anonymous commentator’s reading, stands for an ablative ‘from death’
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «मृत्युर्व्यत्ययेन मृत्योः सकाशान्मे मां पाहि» — nominative for ablative by exchange of case

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: namaḥ + rudrāya → namo rudrāya: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant.

sandhi.type: visarga after u before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: mṛtyuḥ + me → mṛtyur me: after u the visarga becomes r.

morphology.note: Grammatically a nominative, which does not fit the imperative pāhi addressed to ‘you’. The anonymous commentator explains it as standing for the ablative by exchange of case (vyatyaya): ‘protect me from death’.
The enclitic of the first person, here used for the accusative ‘me’, as the anonymous commentator glosses it.

translation.literal: Homage to Rudra, to Viṣṇu. Death — protect me.
translation.readable: Homage to Rudra, homage to Viṣṇu. Protect me from death.

anvaya: रुद्राय विष्णवे नमः [अस्तु] । मृत्युः मे पाहि
syntax: Two clauses. The first is nominal: namaḥ with two datives and the verb ‘be’ understood. The second is an imperative, pāhi, with the enclitic me as object; mṛtyuḥ does not agree with the second-person verb and is read by the commentator as an ablative.

ambiguities.note: rudrāya viṣṇave may name two deities or one, the second dative in apposition to the first. The anonymous commentator takes two: Rudra, lord of Pārvatī, and Viṣṇu, lord of Lakṣmī, and addresses both.
Read by the anonymous commentator as ‘from death’, by exchange of case.

beginner: This is a single line: homage to Rudra and Viṣṇu, and a request for protection. The last words, read word for word, say ‘death, protect me’. The only commentator in this edition who explains the line, the anonymous one, says that the word for death is to be understood as ‘from death’: the speaker asks the two gods to protect him from death. He takes Rudra and Viṣṇu as two deities and says the formula is meant to ward off death for as long as one lives. In the order of the text it follows the formula said while touching the heart after a meal. The edition reports how the commentator explains the line and makes no claim about what saying it does.
analogy: Like a short signature line under a letter: brief, but it names whom one is writing to and what one asks.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers homage to Rudra and Viṣṇu and asks for protection: the last words read, literally, ‘death, protect me’.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: it follows the address to the heart and is meant to ward off death for as long as one lives («यावज्जीवं मृत्युपरिहारार्थं»). He names the two deities by their consorts: «रुद्राय पार्वतीपतये नमोऽस्तु। विष्णवे लक्ष्मीपतये नमोऽस्तु».

commentary.q: How can ‘death’ be the one asked?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The nominative mṛtyuḥ cannot be the subject of the second-person pāhi. The anonymous commentator explains it as the ablative by exchange of case: «मृत्युर्व्यत्ययेन मृत्योः सकाशान्मे मां पाहि» — protect me from death.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources: Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available, and the commentaries present (the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara) are ritual and Vedic explanations, not school readings. Only the anonymous commentator explains this formula in the edition’s sources.

contemporary.text: A daily formula that names death plainly and asks for protection keeps the fact of mortality within ordinary life rather than outside it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a short prayer name death directly instead of avoiding the word?
reflect.deeper: The commentator reads ‘death’ as ‘from death’. What would the line mean if it were read as an address to Death itself?
reflect.practice: Notice one moment today when you take your own safety for granted.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa or of Bhāskara on this formula is in the edition’s files; their recensions, as available here, do not contain it.

flags.note: One deity or two, and mṛtyuḥ as ‘from death’: the reading is the anonymous commentator’s.
Only one commentary explains this anuvāka in the edition’s sources.
